messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was fifty-five when he finally walked into a therapist's office, though the beating that shaped his life had occurred more than half a century earlier. He was seven years old when his stepfather—a man whose name he had learned to associate with the sound of a belt being unbuckled—came home one evening in a rage. Marcus had left a toy on the kitchen floor. The punishment that followed was not a single blow but a sustained assault, the kind that leaves a child unable to construct a coherent narrative of what happened, only fragments: the kitchen tiles against his cheek, the smell of his stepfather's cologne mixed with alcohol, a voice saying things he had learned to forget. For decades, when Marcus tried to recall that evening clearly, the details scattered like startled birds. He could remember the toy—a plastic car—but not what came after in any sequence that made sense. Sometimes he could access the memory as though watching a stranger in a film: detached, numb, untethered from the terror that had actually lived in his body that night.

The decades after had taught Marcus to interpret the world through the lens of that violence. He had come to believe, with the certainty of someone who had learned this lesson early, that people could not be trusted. His marriage had collapsed partly because of this: his ex-wife had complained that he could not be close to her, that he flinched at her touch, that he seemed to expect betrayal from her even when she had given him no reason. When she left, Marcus had spent months in a spiral of rumination, replaying the marriage's failures, cataloging his own mistakes and inadequacies alongside a seething inventory of her perceived wrongs. He dwelled on both with equal intensity, unable to stop the loop.

His work as a fashion designer had once been a refuge. The precision required, the ability to control every element of a garment's construction, had felt like a counterweight to the chaos of his inner life. But over the past two years, his concentration had fractured. He found himself avoiding certain times of day—particularly early evenings, when his stepfather used to return from work—because he knew they would trigger nightmares. He had begun scheduling his design work only in the mornings and afternoons, which meant missing client meetings and collaborative sessions. His reputation, once stellar, had begun to slip. Colleagues noticed he was less available. A younger designer had been given the lead on a major collection that Marcus would once have fought for.

At home, Marcus felt perpetually vigilant. Even in his own apartment, he could not relax. He would sit in his study with the door locked, alert to every sound in the hallway, every shift in the ambient noise of the building. When silence fell—the kind of heavy, expectant silence that sometimes occurs in the late evening—he became convinced that something terrible was about to happen. His body would tense, his breathing would shallow, and he would wait for the blow he knew was coming, even though he also knew, intellectually, that he was safe.

What terrified him most was the possibility that he was losing his mind. His reactions felt uncontrollable, disproportionate to his actual circumstances. When his upstairs neighbor knocked on his door last month to ask about a water leak, Marcus had jerked away from the unexpected touch on his shoulder with such violence that he had nearly fallen. The fear that seized him was primal and total. Afterward, alone, he had sat on his bed and thought: *This is madness. Normal people don't react like this. I am broken in some fundamental way that cannot be fixed.*

It was his sister who finally convinced him to call a therapist. She had told him, gently but directly, that she was worried about him, that she had watched him withdraw further each year, that his isolation was complete. Marcus had resisted for weeks, but the weight of his own thoughts—the endless rumination, the nightmares, the conviction that he had been permanently altered by what had happened to him—had finally become unbearable. He was not sure a therapist could help someone as damaged as he believed himself to be, but he had run out of ways to manage alone.
